And for this reason black bile took hold of him,
and he began to imagine vile fantasies,
and to deem himself to be God.
And because the intellect of those who were under his hand was darkened in great error,
and they were given over to a useless mind,
they believed everything he would say.
And no one dared to admonish him;
rather, anyone who blamed and exposed him,
they would put to a cruel death.
And on this account even certain wise men who were bound to his service,
out of their fear, magnified him as though he were God.
Now by nature that Ala al-Din hated ornaments;
for he used to wear clothing of wool and blue camlet,
and he constantly tended sheep.
It is related
that on one of the days,
while he was sitting upon the edge of a certain high mountain,
and ambassadors from the kings of the regions were with him,
at a mere nod of his eyebrow, fifty men of those who were standing before him threw themselves down from the edge of that high mountain and died.
And thus his fear fell upon all the kings of the earth,
and they were subjugated under the yoke of tribute, which they would give and send to him together with the choice goods of their lands.
And in the year
six hundred and twenty-one
(621 of the Arabs), al-Malik al-Afdal, son of Salah al-Din, son of Ayyub, the lord of Samosata, died in Samosata itself.
This man was very well versed in books, elegance of speech, and poetry,
but he was weak in his governance
and devoid of the cunning
that is necessary for kings.
And for this reason he was deprived
of the kingdom of his father,
and against his will he took a small fortress instead of that great dominion.
And in the year six hundred and twenty-two
(622), the Caliph al-Nasir Abu'l-Abbas Ahmad died, being seventy years old,
on the night that ushered in the feast of the Passover of the Arabs [Eid al-Fitr].
For he was very vigilant and zealous,
and he used constantly to disguise himself and go out wandering through the markets of Baghdad.
And he took care to know, from a thread to a needle,
the affairs of both the great and the small.
At times he would appear in the guise of Turks,
and at times in the guise of Persians,
and at times in the guise of merchants.
